Selective silencing of proprioceptive afferents innervating the forelimb will reduce M1 pre-movement depolarization, depolarize the reach reversal potential, and weaken fast membrane potential–kinematic correlations, demonstrating that proprioceptive feedback is the principal sensory driver of cortical sensorimotor dynamics during voluntary reaching.

The hyperpolarized reach reversal potential in layer 2/3 motor cortex is generated by feedforward recruitment of parvalbumin-positive interneurons via somatosensory cortex inputs, such that selective optogenetic suppression of these interneurons during reaching shifts the reversal potential toward the depolarized values observed following dorsal rhizotomy.

Activation of parvalbumin-positive fast-spiking interneurons in M1 layer 2/3 is necessary for the somatosensory input-dependent hyperpolarization of the reach reversal potential during voluntary forelimb reaching.

Selective suppression of parvalbumin-positive interneurons in forelimb motor cortex will eliminate the somatosensory-driven hyperpolarization during reaching and shift the reach reversal potential toward more depolarized values, thereby impairing reach precision in otherwise intact mice.

Selective optogenetic silencing of proprioceptive, but not tactile, forelimb afferents during the pre-movement period will abolish the early pre-movement membrane potential depolarization in layer 2/3 motor cortex without eliminating centrally-generated cortical state transitions, resulting in delayed reach initiation and reduced reach precision.

Optogenetic activation of parvalbumin-positive interneurons in layer 2/3 of forelimb motor cortex is sufficient to restore the hyperpolarized reach reversal potential and improve the precision and speed of forelimb reaches in mice with deafferented forelimbs.

Selective optogenetic silencing of proprioceptive, but not tactile, forelimb somatosensory afferents during reaching will shift the reach reversal potential in M1 layer 2/3 neurons toward more depolarized values and reduce the trial-by-trial correlation between membrane potential and forelimb distance, without abolishing centrally generated quiet-to-move state transitions.

Forelimb proprioceptive input conveyed by muscle spindle afferents is the primary driver of the hyperpolarized reach reversal potential in M1 layer 2/3 by recruiting parvalbumin-positive interneurons during voluntary reaching.
